text: If some straight-line touches a circle, and some (other) straight-line is drawn across, from the point of contact into the circle, cutting the circle (in two), (then) those angles the (straight-line) makes with the tangent will be equal to the angles in the alternate segments of the circle. For let some straight-line $EF$ touch the circle $ABCD$ at the point $B$, and let some (other) straight-line $BD$ be drawn from point $B$ into the circle $ABCD$, cutting it (in two). I say that the angles $BD$ makes with the tangent $EF$ will be equal to the angles in the alternate segments of the circle. That is to say, that angle $FBD$ is equal to the angle constructed in segment $BAD$, and angle $EBD$ is equal to the angle constructed in segment $DCB$.
For let $BA$ be drawn from $B$, at right-angles to $EF$ [Prop.~1.11].
And let the point $C$ be taken at random on the circumference $BD$.

And since some straight-line $EF$ touches the circle $ABCD$ at point $B$, and $BA$ has been drawn from the point of contact, at right-angles to the tangent, the center of circle $ABCD$ is thus on $BA$ [Prop.~3.19].
assertion: center of circle ABCD is on BA

spans.label: assumption
spans.text: some straight-line $EF$ touches the circle $ABCD$ at point $B$

spans.label: assumption
spans.text: $BA$ has been drawn from the point of contact, at right-angles to the tangent

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the center of circle $ABCD$ is thus on $BA$

text: Thus, $BA$ is a diameter of circle $ABCD$.
assertion: BA is a diameter of circle ABCD

text: Thus, angle $ADB$, being in a semi-circle, is a right-angle [Prop.~3.31].

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: angle $ADB$, being in a semi-circle, is a right-angle

text: Thus, the remaining angles (of triangle $ADB$) $BAD$ and $ABD$ are equal to one right-angle [Prop.~1.32].
assertion: angles BAD and ABD sum to one right-angle

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the remaining angles (of triangle $ADB$) $BAD$ and $ABD$ are equal to one right-angle

text: Thus, the remaining angle $DBF$ is equal to the angle $BAD$ in the alternate segment of the circle.
assertion: angle DBF = angle BAD in alternate segment

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the remaining angle $DBF$ is equal to the angle $BAD$ in the alternate segment of the circle

text: And since $ABCD$ is a quadrilateral in a circle, (the sum of) its opposite angles is equal to two right-angles [Prop.~3.22].
assertion: opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral ABCD sum to two right-angles

spans.label: assumption
spans.text: $ABCD$ is a quadrilateral in a circle

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: (the sum of) its opposite angles is equal to two right-angles

text: And $DBF$ and $DBE$ is also equal to two right-angles [Prop.~1.13].

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: $DBF$ and $DBE$ is also equal to two right-angles

text: Thus, $DBF$ and $DBE$ is equal to $BAD$ and $BCD$, of which $BAD$ was shown (to be) equal to $DBF$.
Thus, the remaining (angle) $DBE$ is equal to the angle $DCB$ in the alternate segment $DCB$ of the circle.
assertion: angle DBE = angle DCB in alternate segment DCB

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the remaining (angle) $DBE$ is equal to the angle $DCB$ in the alternate segment $DCB$ of the circle

text: Thus, if some straight-line touches a circle, and some (other) straight-line is drawn across, from the point of contact into the circle, cutting the circle (in two), (then) those angles the (straight-line) makes with the tangent will be equal to the angles in the alternate segments of the circle. (Which is) the very thing it was required to show.
